hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, grayscale visual patterns characterized by deep black or charcoal-gray masses juxtaposed against bright white or light gray regions. The core driver is the sharp luminance boundary or polarity between a substantial dark area—such as black fur, plumage, deep shadows, or painted metal—and a lighter adjacent area or background, often manifesting as organic curves, silhouettes, or glossy surfaces with specular highlights. The neuron is invariant to object identity (activating for birds, mammals, snakes, and man-made objects), texture, and lighting direction, provided the intense dark–light tonal contrast is preserved. The activating features typically occupy 30–70% of the image area, often oriented diagonally or vertically and positioned centrally or slightly off-center. The visual palette is consistently achromatic, featuring jet black and dark gray elements set against or interspersed with bright white, off-white, or medium gray tones.
